title: Automate enquiry follow-up so no quote goes quiet
h1: How to automate enquiry follow-up without losing the personal touch
desc: Enquiry follow-up can be automated. A system reads the inbox, quotes and invoices, finds what went quiet and drafts replies a person approves before sending.
lead: Enquiry follow-up can be automated with a system that reads the inbox, the quotes and the invoices, finds every conversation that went quiet, and drafts the next reply. A person reads each draft and approves it, and only then does it go. Nothing slips, and nothing leaves that the team hasn't seen.
short: Most lost work isn't refused. It goes quiet.
The system reads the inbox, quotes and invoices, and lists everything still waiting on a reply.
It drafts each follow-up in the firm's own voice, with the context attached.
A thread drops off the list as soon as the client replies, books, pays or says no.

sections.h2: Why do enquiries and quotes go quiet?
body: An enquiry lands on a busy Tuesday. Someone answers it, sends a quote, and means to check back. Then other work arrives and the thread sinks under newer mail. Nobody decided to drop it. Looking again was nobody's job.

It happens everywhere, from an independent professional to an established firm with a shared inbox. The more people share an inbox, the easier it is for each of them to assume someone else is chasing. The cost doesn't show up anywhere obvious. It's work the firm was close to winning, lost without anyone ever saying no.
Follow-up runs on memory, which is why it suits a system. Let the system do the remembering and the drafting, and leave the final word with a person.

sections.h2: What does an automated follow-up system actually do?
body: The system Loose Ends builds works inside the tools the firm already has. The inbox and the accounting tool stay where they are. It reads them and keeps a list of what needs attention:
Reads the inbox for enquiries and the replies to them.
Reads sent quotes and open invoices, so it knows what was offered and what's still unpaid.
Finds every conversation where the firm sent the last message and nothing came back.
Drafts a follow-up for each one, referring to what was actually discussed.
Puts the drafts in a queue for someone to read, edit, approve or discard.
Sends only what was approved, from the firm's own address.
Each morning there's a short list waiting, instead of a dig through old threads. The team stops retyping the same chasing email and starts reviewing drafts that are ready to go.

sections.h2: How does the system decide what has gone quiet?
body: The firm sets the rules in plain terms during the build. One rule might say a quote with no reply after a set number of days gets followed up. Another might flag an enquiry that was answered once and never acknowledged.

Different work can follow different rules. A large proposal might deserve a longer pause than a quick price question. A returning client might get a warmer note than a first-time enquiry. All the rules sit in one place, so changing them later doesn't mean rebuilding anything.
It also knows when to stop. If the client replied, booked, paid or said no, the thread leaves the list. Nobody gets chased twice, and the queue stays honest.

sections.h2: Who approves the follow-up before it is sent?
body: A named person on the team approves each message. Every system Loose Ends builds works this way. The system drafts and prepares, and a person signs off before anything reaches a client.

When the draft is good, approval is quick. The original enquiry, the quote, the date of the last message and the proposed reply all sit on one screen. The person can send it as it is, change a line, or let the thread rest.

There's more to this step than safety. A follow-up is part of a relationship, and the person approving it might know the client is travelling this week, or that a phone call would land better. The system can't know that, and it doesn't pretend to.

sections.h2: What does a good follow-up draft look like?
body: Short, specific, and written in the firm's own tone. It mentions the actual work discussed and asks one clear question that's easy to answer. A good draft:
Names the quote or request it refers to.
Repeats the one detail the client is most likely to need.
Offers an easy next step, like a time to talk or a yes or no.
Sounds like the person who wrote the first message.
During the build, the studio collects examples of how the team already writes, so the drafts match. If one reads wrong, the person approving it corrects it, and the examples get updated.

A draft also has to know what to leave out. It won't invent a discount, promise a date nobody agreed, or guess at a detail missing from the thread. If something's unclear, it leaves a note for the approver and the gap stays open.

sections.h2: Which tools can it connect to?
body: It connects to email, calendar, spreadsheets and the firm's accounting or quoting tool. Where a Claude connector exists, it uses one. Those connectors are built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard Anthropic introduced in November 2024 for connecting AI assistants to tools and data. Where there's no connector, Loose Ends writes a custom connection to the tool's API.
The firm owns all of it, from the code and accounts to the data. The build is agreed at one fixed price in writing, and at handover every routine has a named owner on the team.

The approval queue can live wherever the team already works. For some firms that's the inbox, with drafts waiting in a folder. For others it's a Slack channel or a plain internal page. Approving a follow-up should take no more effort than reading an email.

sections.h2: Where should a firm start?
body: Start by listing where enquiries and quotes arrive and who's expected to chase them. That alone often shows where things go quiet. A paid audit can then rank the first fixes, with the fee credited toward the build. For a first look at where following up, confirming or chasing costs the firm time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, and no call is required.

faq.q: Does automated follow-up send emails on its own?
faq.a: No. Each follow-up is drafted and placed in a queue, and someone approves it before it goes.

faq.q: Can it follow up on quotes as well as enquiries?
faq.a: Yes. It reads sent quotes and open invoices alongside the inbox, so a quote with no reply turns up as easily as an unanswered enquiry.

faq.q: Will the messages sound like a template?
faq.a: They're written from the actual thread and from examples of how the team already writes. The approver can change any line before it goes.

faq.q: Does the firm have to change its email or accounting tool?
faq.a: No. The system works inside the existing tools and connects to them through connectors or custom API connections.

title: Automate invoice reminders with a person approving each one
h1: How to automate invoice reminders and keep the tone right
desc: Invoice reminders can run on a schedule. The system checks the accounting tool, drafts a reminder for each stage, and a person approves it before it goes out.
lead: Invoice reminders can be automated by connecting the accounting tool to email and letting a system check, on a schedule, which invoices are due or overdue. At each stage it drafts a reminder in the right tone, and a person approves it before it's sent. The chasing happens on time, and nobody has to remember to do it.
short: Open invoices are checked on a set schedule.
Each stage has its own tone, from a friendly note to a firmer request.
Clients who need a personal word can be marked for a person to handle.
Paid invoices drop off the list by themselves.

sections.h2: Why is chasing invoices so easy to put off?
body: Nobody likes chasing an unpaid invoice. It interrupts other work. It means opening the accounting tool, finding the invoice, checking whether someone already chased it, and writing an email that's polite but clear. So it waits for the end of the month.

By then several invoices are late at once, and the reminders go out in a rush, in an uneven tone. Some clients get chased twice and others get missed. Cash arrives later than it should, and the relationship picks up an awkward edge it didn't need.

It's rarely that nobody cares. Chasing depends on someone remembering to look, at the right moment, in a tool they don't open every day. A scheduled system is good at exactly that, as long as a person still decides what gets sent.

sections.h2: How does scheduled invoice follow-up work?
body: The system Loose Ends builds reads the firm's accounting tool on a regular schedule. It looks at every open invoice, its due date and its reminder history, works out which ones need a message today, and drafts that message. On each run it:
Checks open invoices and their due dates.
Works out which stage each invoice has reached.
Drafts the reminder for that stage, with the invoice number, amount and a link to pay.
Puts each draft in a queue for someone to approve, edit or hold.
Sends approved reminders from the firm's own email address.
Records what went out, so the next stage starts from the right point.
Once the accounting tool shows an invoice as paid, it leaves the list. Nobody gets a reminder for a bill they've already settled.

sections.h2: What stages should invoice reminders follow?
body: The firm picks the stages and timing during the build. A common pattern starts with a gentle note shortly before the due date and a polite reminder soon after it. If the invoice stays unpaid, a clearer request follows. The last message hands the matter to a named person on the team.

Each stage has its own wording. Early messages assume an oversight. Later ones are more direct about dates and next steps. The last stage doesn't threaten anything by itself. It brings a person in, because a long overdue invoice usually needs a conversation more than another email.
All the stages are kept in one place, so they can be changed without rebuilding the system.

Every reminder carries what the client needs to act straight away, which is the invoice number, the amount, the original due date and a way to pay. A clear reminder gets answered sooner than a vague one, and the client doesn't have to write back asking which invoice is meant.

sections.h2: How is the tone kept right for each client?
body: Not every client should be chased the same way. A long-standing client with one late invoice deserves different words from an account that's often late. So the system can hold notes for each client, such as:
A preferred contact name.
The client's usual payment pattern, so the timing fits.
A request to always copy someone in the client's accounts team.
Accounts that should always be handled by a person and never drafted.
Phrases the firm uses, and phrases it never uses.
Whoever approves a reminder sees these notes beside the draft. If something feels off, they change it or hold it.

sections.h2: Why does a person approve every reminder?
body: A reminder about money goes straight to the heart of a client relationship. The system can see dates and amounts. It can't see that the client rang yesterday to say payment is on its way, or that a dispute is open. A person can.

So every system Loose Ends builds drafts first and waits for approval before anything reaches a client. When the draft is right, approval takes a moment, and it catches the cases where sending would be a mistake. The team still decides. It just doesn't have to remember anymore.

The queue can sit where the team already works. Some firms like a daily email listing the reminders waiting, with a button to approve each one. Others prefer a Slack channel or a short page inside an internal tool. Either way, the invoice, its history and the draft appear together, so the decision is quick.

sections.h2: Which accounting and email tools can it connect to?
body: It connects to the firm's accounting or invoicing tool, its email and, where it helps, a spreadsheet or a Slack channel for the approval queue. Where a Claude connector exists, the studio uses it. Connectors are built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard Anthropic introduced in November 2024. If there's none, Loose Ends builds a custom connection to the tool's API.
Code, accounts and data belong to the firm. At handover the team is trained, and a named person owns the routine.
The same connection can feed a short weekly view of what's outstanding, too. The team sees at a glance which invoices are waiting and which reminders went out.

sections.h2: How should a firm get started?
body: Write down how invoices get chased today. Who does it, when, and with what wording. The gaps usually show up straight away. A paid audit can then rank the first fixes, with the fee credited toward a build at one fixed price. For a first look at where following up, confirming or chasing costs the firm time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Will clients receive reminders automatically without anyone checking?
faq.a: No. Every reminder is drafted and queued, and a person approves it before it's sent.

faq.q: What happens when a client pays?
faq.a: The system reads the accounting tool, so once an invoice is marked paid it leaves the list and no more reminders are drafted.
Yes. Any client can be marked as person-only. The system flags their invoices without drafting anything.

title: Booking confirmation and reminder automation, explained
h1: How to automate booking confirmations, reminders and rescheduling
desc: Booking confirmations, reminders and rescheduling can run by themselves once bookings live in one place instead of in direct messages. Here's how it works.
lead: Booking confirmations, reminders and rescheduling can be automated once every booking lives in one place, instead of being spread across direct messages, emails and a paper diary. The booking system confirms each place, sends a reminder before the session, and lets the client move or cancel through a link. Nobody on the team has to answer, confirm or reschedule by hand.
short: Bookings first have to leave direct messages and sit in one place.
Confirmations and reminders then go out by themselves, using set wording.
Clients reschedule through a link, within rules the business sets.
Anything unusual goes to a person to decide.

sections.h2: Why do bookings through direct messages cause problems?
body: Lots of businesses start by taking bookings wherever clients write in. Instagram, WhatsApp, email, a phone call. It works for a while. Then someone has to read every message, reply, check the diary, confirm, and remember to send a reminder.

Messages get missed. Places get counted twice. Whoever answers spends evenings confirming when they could be working, payment gets chased separately, and every reschedule is another round of messages. None of it is hard. All of it is manual, and it lands on whoever holds the phone.

Clients feel it too. A booking that depends on a reply can wait hours for confirmation, and someone unsure they have a place may book elsewhere. A clear confirmation that arrives straight away is good service as much as a saving for the team.

sections.h2: What can booking automation handle on its own?
body: Once bookings sit in one system, most routine messages can go out without anyone typing them. They're factual, with set wording the business approved once:
A confirmation as soon as a place is booked and paid.
A reminder before the session, with the time, place and anything to bring.
A link to reschedule or cancel, within the business's rules.
A notice to the next person on a waiting list when a place opens.
An update to the team's calendar or schedule whenever something changes.
Since a person wrote and approved the wording of each message once, at setup, these notices can go out by themselves. Anything that isn't routine gets handled differently.

Keep each message to what the client needs. The session, the date and time, the address, what to bring, how to change the booking. Short notices get read, and they head off the questions that would otherwise come back as more messages to answer.

sections.h2: What should stay with a person?
body: Some booking messages aren't routine at all. A complaint. A refund request outside the rules. A question about health or access, or a group booking on special terms. These need a human answer.

The system flags them and drafts a reply where it can, and a person approves it before it reaches the client. Loose Ends applies this rule everywhere. Fixed notices approved in advance can go out alone, and everything else waits for someone to read it.
It matters for the tone of the business, too. A reminder can be automatic. An apology shouldn't be.

Each flagged message shows up with the booking, the client's history and a suggested reply on one screen. Whoever's deciding reads, adjusts and sends, without digging through old conversations to work out what happened.

sections.h2: How did a yoga studio move its bookings out of Instagram?
body: A yoga studio was taking bookings through Instagram messages. Loose Ends built a booking application that puts the schedule, the available places and payment on a single phone screen, in French and English.

Clients now see the classes, pick a place and pay in one step, with no message to write. Bookings moved out of Instagram messages into one place, where the studio can see who's coming to each class. The application is live.
Contact with clients was never the problem. The aim was to stop the studio's messages from doubling as a booking diary, so conversations there can be about practice instead of places.
Two languages were part of the brief from the start. Clients choose French or English, and the schedule, the confirmation and the payment step all follow in that language.

sections.h2: How does rescheduling work without back-and-forth?
body: Rescheduling is where manual booking eats the most time. One change can take several messages to find a new slot. With a single booking system, the client opens a link, sees what's free and moves the booking, inside limits the business has set, such as:
How close to the session a booking can still be moved.
Whether a late cancellation keeps or releases the payment.
How many times one booking can be moved.
Which sessions can only be changed by a person.
If a change falls outside those rules, the system passes it to the team and leaves the decision there.

A released place can go to the waiting list straight away. The next person gets a notice and a link, and the class fills again without anyone on the team writing to anyone. If nobody takes it, the place goes back on the public schedule.

sections.h2: Which tools does a booking system connect to?
body: A booking application can connect to the business's calendar, its payment provider, its email and, where useful, a spreadsheet the team already plans with. It can also sit inside an existing website. Loose Ends builds the application to order, or connects existing tools where they already do the job.
Code, domain and accounts belong to the business, and the build is agreed at one fixed price in writing.

At handover the team is trained, and a named person owns each routine, from the reminder wording to the rescheduling rules. Changes after launch, like a new class or a new cancellation policy, are made in one place and apply everywhere.

sections.h2: Where should a business begin?
body: List every place a booking can arrive today and every message the team sends about it. The list is usually longer than anyone expects, and it shows what to fix first. For a first look at where following up, confirming or chasing costs the business time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Do clients need to download an app to book?
faq.a: Not necessarily. A booking application can open in the phone's browser from a link, so clients book on one screen without installing anything.

faq.q: Can confirmations and reminders be sent automatically?
faq.a: Yes. A person writes and approves their wording once, at setup. Messages that aren't routine, like replies to complaints, are drafted and approved by a person before they go.

faq.q: Can the booking system work in more than one language?
faq.a: Yes. The yoga studio's booking application, for example, works in French and English.

faq.q: What if a client wants to reschedule outside the rules?
faq.a: The request goes to a person on the team, who decides and replies.

title: Human-in-the-loop automation: approve before it sends
h1: Human-in-the-loop automation: why every system should draft first
desc: Human-in-the-loop automation means the system drafts and a person approves before anything reaches a client. Where approval sits, and what never to automate.
lead: Human-in-the-loop automation means the system does the reading, sorting and drafting, and a person approves before anything reaches a client. The firm keeps the time automation saves, without the risk of a wrong message going out under its name. Loose Ends builds every system this way.
short: The system prepares, and a person approves anything a client will see.
Internal chores can often run fully by themselves.
Some decisions should never be automated, whatever the tool.
Approval is also how mistakes get caught and the system gets better.

sections.h2: What does human-in-the-loop automation mean?
body: A person stays in the process at the point where it counts. The system handles the slow work, like reading the inbox, finding what needs attention, pulling figures and drafting the reply. A person reads the result and decides whether it goes.
Some automation runs end to end with no review. That's fine for some jobs and wrong for others. So the useful question is where the person belongs, more than whether to automate at all.

Most of the time in a routine goes into finding and preparing. Approving a ready reply takes moments. Finding the thread, checking the quote and writing the reply from scratch takes far longer. Human-in-the-loop automation removes the slow part and leaves the decision where it was.

sections.h2: Why should a system draft first instead of sending?
body: Anything sent to a client speaks for the firm. A system can read the facts in front of it, but it can't know everything the team knows. That a client called this morning. That a project is sensitive. That a certain phrase will land badly.

Drafting first keeps the speed of automation and keeps the firm's voice with the firm. The approver isn't facing a blank page. They read, adjust and send. A good draft takes a moment to approve, and a bad one stops right there.
It also builds trust. A team that sees every draft for the first few weeks learns fast what the system does well and where its rules need work.

sections.h2: Where should the approval step sit?
body: Put approval at the last point before something leaves the firm, and nowhere it isn't needed. Too many approval steps and people stop reading them. Too few and something slips through. The places it belongs:
Before any email, message or document is sent to a client.
Before anything is published under the firm's name, such as a post or an article.
Before money moves, such as a refund or a payment run.
Before a record is changed in a way that's hard to undo.
The approval screen should show everything needed to decide, meaning the original message, the context the system used, and the draft. Nobody should have to open several tools to approve one reply.

The queue can live wherever the team already works. A folder of drafts in the inbox, a Slack channel, a plain internal page. What matters is that it's checked at a set time each day and one named person is responsible for it.

sections.h2: What can be automated fully?
body: Work that stays inside the firm and can be checked later is usually safe to run alone. Copying data from one tool to another. Filing documents into the right folder. Preparing a weekly figures summary for the team, or adding a new booking to the calendar.

Fixed notices whose wording a person already approved, like a booking confirmation or a reminder before a session, can go out alone as well. The approval happened once, at setup, and the message doesn't change.

A handy test is to ask what happens if the system gets it wrong. If someone on the team would notice and fix it with no harm done, the job can usually run by itself. If a client would receive something wrong, or money would move, a person approves first.

sections.h2: What should never be automated?
body: Some decisions belong to people, however good the tools get. Loose Ends doesn't build systems that make these alone:
Hiring decisions. In Vero, the studio's own recruiting software, the system ranks candidates and shows its reasoning, and the decision stays with the recruiter.
Replies to complaints, disputes or anything sensitive.
Changes to prices, terms or contracts.
Anything that fills a gap in the facts with a guess.

That last one shapes how the studio's systems are built. They flag a gap and leave it open. A report built from interview notes, for example, points every rating to its source and marks what's missing.

ZonedInOut, the studio's own scoring product, follows the same thinking. It scores stocks, funds and cryptocurrencies each trading day, and it publishes and grades its past calls. It's a scoring system, not financial advice, and the decision to act stays with the person.

sections.h2: How are mistakes caught?
body: The approval step catches most mistakes before they matter. The rest of the design makes the others easier to see. Every draft shows where its facts came from. Every score or rating points to the source text behind it. Every message sent is recorded, so the team can look back.

When someone edits a draft, that edit tells the owner something useful. If the same correction keeps coming up, the rules or examples behind the drafts get updated. Over time the drafts need fewer changes, and approval stays quick.
At handover every routine has a named owner on the team. There's always one person who knows how it works and notices when something looks off.

sections.h2: How does a firm decide where to start?
body: List the chores the team repeats each week, then mark the ones that send something to a client. Those get a draft and an approval step. The rest may run alone. For a first look at where following up, confirming or chasing costs the firm time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Does human-in-the-loop automation slow things down?
faq.a: Very little, when the drafts are good. The approver reads and sends instead of writing from scratch, and the system has already done the slow part.

faq.q: Can some messages go out without approval?
faq.a: Fixed notices whose wording was approved once at setup, like booking confirmations, can. Anything written for a specific client is approved by a person first.
A named person on the team, agreed at handover. Every routine has an owner, so approvals don't fall between people.

title: Automate weekly reporting: figures ready before anyone asks
h1: How to automate weekly reporting from the tools a firm already uses
desc: Weekly reporting can be automated by pulling figures from existing tools into one dashboard and sending the team a short summary in Slack or email each week.
lead: Weekly reporting can be automated by connecting the tools that already hold the figures, gathering them into one dashboard, and sending the team a short written summary on a set day. The numbers are ready before anyone asks. Nobody loses a Monday morning copying figures between tabs.
short: Figures come straight from the tools the firm already uses.
One dashboard shows them in the same place every week.
A short summary reaches the team in Slack or by email.
Missing or odd figures are flagged and never filled with a guess.

sections.h2: Why does weekly reporting take so long?
body: The figures a team needs each week tend to live in several places. Sales in one tool, bookings in another, invoices in the accounting system, enquiries in the inbox, campaign results somewhere else again. Someone opens each one, copies the numbers into a spreadsheet, checks them, and writes a few lines on what changed.
That's retyping. Figures get copied wrong, and the report often arrives late, after someone has already asked for it. When the usual person is away, it doesn't get done.

So the meeting opens with questions about the numbers when it should be about what to do next. Time goes into finding figures instead of reading them. The report is needed. The copying behind it doesn't need a person.

sections.h2: What does automated weekly reporting look like?
body: The system Loose Ends builds connects to each source, collects the agreed figures on a schedule and puts them in one dashboard. Then it writes a short summary of what moved and sends it to the team. Each week it:
Reads figures from each connected tool on a set day and time.
Stores them, so each week can be compared with the last.
Updates one dashboard the whole team can open.
Writes a short summary of what changed and what needs a look.
Sends the summary to a Slack channel or by email.
Flags any figure that's missing or outside its usual range.
Both the dashboard and the summary are built around the questions the team actually asks each week. Numbers nobody asks about stay out.
Because the figures are collected the same way every week, the comparison is fair. When a figure moves, the business moved. Who copied it, and with which filter, stops mattering.

sections.h2: Which figures should a weekly report include?
body: Fewer than most teams expect. A weekly report earns its place when it can be read in a minute and acted on. The right figures depend on the business, but they usually answer a few plain questions:
What came in: new enquiries, bookings or orders.
What went out: quotes sent, invoices issued, work delivered.
What is waiting: unpaid invoices, unanswered enquiries, open tasks.
What changed compared with last week, and why that might be.
During the build the studio agrees each figure with the team, including exactly where it comes from, so everyone reads it the same way.

The summary is written in sentences, since another table wouldn't help anyone. It might say that enquiries rose on last week, that a few invoices passed their due date, and that one figure couldn't be read. Each line links to the dashboard for anyone who wants the detail.

sections.h2: Which tools can the figures come from?
body: Most tools a firm already uses can supply figures. Accounting and invoicing tools, Shopify and Etsy for online shops, booking systems, spreadsheets and databases, email, calendars, and recruiting systems such as Loxo. Where a Claude connector exists, the studio uses it. Connectors are built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard Anthropic introduced in November 2024 for connecting AI assistants to tools and data.
Where there's no connector, Loose Ends builds a custom connection to the tool's API. Nothing has to be replaced, and the firm keeps ownership of the code, the accounts and the data.

sections.h2: Who checks the summary before it is shared?
body: A summary that stays inside the team can usually go out by itself. It's prepared from the firm's own figures, and the team reads it as a starting point. Each figure links back to its source, so anyone can check it.
If the summary goes outside the firm, say to a client, a partner or a board, it's drafted first and a person approves it before it's sent. That's the rule in every system the studio builds.
Either way, a gap never gets filled with a guess. If a figure couldn't be read, the summary says so.

Each figure on the dashboard also shows when it was last updated and which tool it came from. It's a small detail that saves a lot of doubt. When a number looks odd, the team can see at once whether the business changed or the source did.

sections.h2: Can the team ask questions about the figures?
body: Yes, if the data is also connected to the team's AI assistant. With the figures in one place, an assistant such as Claude can be connected to them, and a person can ask a plain question and get an answer drawn from the firm's data.

Setting up AI assistants for a team, connected to its own data, is the studio's main offer. Most teams use only a fraction of what their assistant can do, and a weekly report is often a good first place to close that gap.

At handover the team is trained on the dashboard and the assistant, and a named person owns the weekly routine. If a new figure is needed later, it's added in one place and shows up in both the dashboard and the summary.

sections.h2: Where should a firm start?
body: Write down the figures someone already copies by hand each week, and where each one comes from. That list is the first version of the dashboard. It often shows which figures nobody reads and can be dropped. For a first look at where following up, confirming or chasing costs the firm time, Loose Ends offers a free one-page review, with no call required.

faq.q: Is new software needed for automated reporting?
faq.a: Usually not. The system reads from the tools the firm already uses and gathers the figures into one dashboard.

faq.q: Can the weekly summary be sent to Slack?
faq.a: Yes. It can go to a Slack channel, by email, or both, on a set day each week.

faq.q: What happens if a figure is missing?
faq.a: The summary says the figure couldn't be read and points to the source. It never fills the gap with an estimate.

faq.q: Is the report sent to clients automatically?
faq.a: No. Anything shared outside the firm is drafted first, and a person approves it before it's sent.
